title: Venus and Adonis: Warning and Loss
subtitle: A warning, a hunt, and a flower

learningObjectives.text: What danger does Venus tell Adonis to avoid?
What happens to Adonis's blood in the later episode?

warning.author: Ovid
warning.locator: Book X · Fable IX [X.519-707]; Book X · Fable IX [X.519-707], normalized characters 1723-2214
warning.excerpt: Forbear, youth, to be rash at my hazard, and attack not the wild beasts to which nature has granted arms, lest thy {thirst for} glory should cost me dear. Neither thy age, nor thy beauty, nor {other} things which have made an impression on Venus, make any impression on lions and bristly boars, and the eyes and the tempers of wild beasts. The fierce boars carry lightning[54] in their curving tusks; there is rage and fury unlimited in the tawny lions; and the {whole} race is odious to me.
warning.note: Verbatim translated verse from Ovid. Riley's arguments, synopses, notes, and explanations are separately indexed and are not quoted as primary verse.

flower.author: Ovid
flower.locator: Book X · Fable X [X.708-739]; Book X · Fable X [X.708-739], normalized characters 1254-1745
flower.excerpt: But thy blood shall be changed into a flower. Was it formerly allowed thee, Persephone, to change the limbs[65] of a female into fragrant mint; and shall the hero, the son of Cinyras, {if} changed, be a cause of displeasure against me?’ Having thus said, she sprinkles his blood with odoriferous nectar, which, touched by it, effervesces, just as the transparent bubbles are wont to rise in rainy weather. Nor was there a pause longer than a full hour, when a flower sprang up from the blood

narrativeBlocks.title: Venus warns Adonis
narrativeBlocks.body: Venus warns Adonis against attacking dangerous wild animals, especially boars and lions. Her warning is part of Ovid's narrative of their relationship.

narrativeBlocks.title: The warning names the danger
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Riley's translation; whitespace normalized): “Forbear, youth, to be rash at my hazard, and attack not the wild beasts to which nature has granted arms, lest thy {thirst for} glory should cost me dear. Neither thy age, nor thy beauty, nor {other} things which have made an impression on Venus, make any impression on lions and bristly boars, and the eyes and the tempers of wild beasts. The fierce boars carry lightning[54] in their curving tusks; there is rage and fury unlimited in the tawny lions; and the {whole} race is odious to me.”

narrativeBlocks.title: The warning is not obeyed
narrativeBlocks.body: In the next episode, Adonis is killed by a boar while hunting. Venus says his blood will become a flower and marks his death with mourning.

narrativeBlocks.title: A literary version, not a universal rite
narrativeBlocks.body: The lesson follows Ovid's Book X sequence in Riley's translation. The poem describes Venus's action; it does not prove that every community told the story or marked the death in the same way.

narrativeBlocks.title: Advice and consequence
narrativeBlocks.body: The two passages connect Venus's warning with the later transformation of Adonis's blood into a flower.
